Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

circuitscaper (development version)

New features

  • New dipole methods: connectivity from many balanced source-sink pairs (“dipoles”) superposed on one factored circuit, at a cost of one factorization and a few dozen solves whatever the number of pairs.

    • dp_omni() maps omnidirectional connectivity among habitat, in the role of os_run(), from random-sign dipoles within a radius (in pixels or km): current, flow potential and normalized current, with a built-in estimate of its sampling noise. With a destination, it maps the routes linking two distributions, such as present and future habitat, seasonal ranges, or two habitat types, without direction.
    • dp_pairwise() maps connectivity among every pair of focal nodes, the squared-current analogue of cs_pairwise()’s cumulative map, at a cost independent of the number of nodes, or exactly from one solve per node, with flow potential and normalized current.
    • dp_flux() maps the net flow from an origin to a destination distribution, with direction, in one solve, among pairs within an optional radius, with flow potential and normalized current as in dp_omni(). Its current is the sum of absolute current over a cell’s links, as in Circuitscape, or with cell_value = "rms", the RMS current, as in dp_omni(). Attributes "origin_in_reach" and "destination_in_reach" give the shares of origin and destination strength with any counterpart within the radius, and "pair_weight_in_reach" the share of all origin–destination pair weight within it, which is small whenever the domain is large relative to the radius.
    • dp_directionality() maps both at once from the same pairs, the directional map of dp_flux() and the undirected map of dp_omni(destination = ), with their ratio: where movement between the two distributions is one-way and where it runs both ways. Both it and dp_omni(destination = ) center their random dipoles on the pairs’ mean dipole, which is solved exactly, so their noise is much smaller where movement is one-way.
    • With power = TRUE (off by default), dp_omni(), dp_pairwise(), dp_flux() and dp_directionality() also map the power dissipated, which picks out choke points, and with normalize = TRUE, normalized power. Each link’s squared current is weighted by that link’s resistance, which squaring a current map and multiplying by cell resistance can’t do; it costs no extra solves.
    • dp_isolation() maps how isolated each cell is from its targets, as effective resistance: to the habitat within a radius, or with a destination, between two distributions in both directions (each cell’s resistance to the destination as an origin, and from the origin as a destination). Two layers summarise a cell’s targets: the resistance to them as a set, and the mean resistance to them, each with a normalized version that removes the effect of geometry. Every cell with targets in reach gets a value, habitat or not. Each cell stands for a site of the cells within site_radius (2 pixels by default), since a single cell’s effective resistance is dominated by its own links; site_radius = 0 gives the single-cell reading, and contact = TRUE adds each cell’s exact contact resistance. Random dipoles across every link give these for all cells at once, with per-cell standard errors (se = TRUE). With coverage = TRUE, two more layers compare each cell with ideal continuous habitat at the same radius: coverage, the target strength in reach as a share of the ideal’s, and effective_coverage, coverage discounted by how much harder the targets are to reach than in ideal habitat, which responds to the amount of targets as well as their arrangement and resistance.
    • dp_circuit() prepares a circuit whose factorizations several runs can reuse.
    • The dp_*() functions report progress through the ‘progressr’ package: a step per factorization and, per batch of draws, for sampling the dipoles and for each solve. Wrap a call in progressr::with_progress(), or in a ‘shiny’ app progressr::withProgressShiny(), to see it; with no handler active, nothing is shown. progress = FALSE turns it off. ‘progressr’ is a new dependency.

    These methods map squared current on the whole circuit, so their results differ from Circuitscape’s and Omniscape’s by design; see ?dp_omni. They are experimental.

  • The dipole methods need only Julia, not the Circuitscape and Omniscape Julia packages. cs_install_julia(circuitscape = FALSE) installs Julia alone, and cs_julia_available(circuitscape = FALSE) checks that a recent enough Julia is found and starts.

Changes

  • cs_pairwise() gains normalize, which runs Circuitscape a second time on a uniform surface and adds flow_potential and normalized_current layers to current_map, as in os_run(). It is TRUE by default, for the same default across the package, so cs_pairwise() now takes about twice as long and its current_map has these two extra layers after cumulative_current; set normalize = FALSE for the previous behaviour.

  • cs_setup() now only starts Julia. Circuitscape and Omniscape are loaded and warmed up on the first cs_*() or os_*() call of a session instead, so a session that only uses the dipole methods starts in a few seconds rather than 15 or more. Circuitscape and Omniscape sessions take the same total time as before.

Documentation

  • The getting-started vignette now covers both families of methods, with a guide to choosing one by question. Mode-by-mode material for Circuitscape and Omniscape moved to a website article, beside a new article on the dipole methods: usage, how they work, and how they compare.

Bug fixes

  • cs_setup() now starts Julia when the Julia it finds is a shim or launcher in another directory, such as Chocolatey’s on Windows. It pointed ‘JuliaConnectoR’ at the shim’s directory, which Julia also uses to find its system image, so Julia failed to start (“could not load library …sys.dll”). It now asks Julia for its own directory first.

  • cs_install_julia(force = TRUE) now updates Circuitscape.jl and Omniscape.jl even when a new release needs newer versions of their own dependencies. It previously held those dependencies fixed, so, for example, it stayed on Circuitscape.jl 6.1 instead of installing 6.2, which needs a newer GZip.jl.

  • cs_one_to_all() and cs_all_to_one() return per-node current layers only with cumulative_only = FALSE, as documented. Circuitscape.jl before 6.2 wrote these maps regardless, so with older versions both functions also returned them by default.

circuitscaper 0.2.0

CRAN release: 2026-11-06

New features

  • cs_setup(threads = ) now restarts Julia when it is already running with fewer threads (or with an interactive thread, which breaks parallel runs of Omniscape < 0.6.3), instead of warning that R must be restarted.
  • If the Julia process stops during a session (for example, it crashes or runs out of memory, or is stopped with JuliaConnectoR::stopJulia()), the next circuitscaper call starts and sets up Julia again, instead of failing with connection errors until R is restarted.

Bug fixes

  • circuitscaper now runs Julia in its own process, connected to R by ‘JuliaConnectoR’, instead of inside R’s process via ‘JuliaCall’. With Julia inside R, the libraries R had loaded clashed with the ones Julia bundles, and setup failed on Linux: on Ubuntu 24.04, Julia’s GDAL could not load because terra had already loaded the system libtiff (“version LIBTIFF_4.6.1' not found"), and Julia could also crash on the system libunwind. 'JuliaConnectoR' also starts Julia without R'sLD_LIBRARY_PATH, which crashed Julia's package manager. Julia packages are likewise installed in a separate Julia process with a clean library path. RCall.jl is no longer needed, and the…argument ofcs_setup()(passed toJuliaCall::julia_setup()`) is gone.

  • The shell and Julia commands circuitscaper runs to find and check Julia (including at package attach) now time out instead of potentially hanging, e.g. on a slow login shell profile.

  • cs_setup() and cs_install_julia() now refuse Julia versions older than 1.10 with an explanation of how to upgrade. On older Julia, the package manager falls back to old releases of Circuitscape.jl and Omniscape.jl that fail in obscure ways. The minimum in SystemRequirements is now Julia 1.10.

  • cs_install_julia() now downloads and installs Julia itself, from the official release index at julialang.org, verifying each download against its published size and (on R >= 4.5) SHA-256 checksum. Julia goes into circuitscaper’s user data directory (tools::R_user_dir("circuitscaper")) and is found automatically by cs_setup(). Previously it used JuliaCall::install_julia(), which in the current CRAN release of ‘JuliaCall’ (0.17.6) installs Julia 1.9 when asked for the latest version and can’t install Julia 1.10 or later, so a fresh install failed with errors such as “undefined symbol: SET_SYMVALUE”.

  • cs_setup() now starts the Julia it finds explicitly, so the Julia whose version it checks is always the one that starts, and stops with a clear message if an older Julia is already running in the session.

  • cs_setup() now finds Julia wherever JuliaCall::julia_setup() would, instead of only on the PATH. Previously, a Julia installed by cs_install_julia() (which JuliaCall::install_julia() places outside the PATH) was not found in later sessions, so cs_setup() failed with “Julia not found” until julia_home was given explicitly. The same applied to Julia installed via juliaup or Homebrew when R was started from the macOS GUI, whose PATH lacks the shell’s. cs_install_julia(), cs_julia_available(), and the startup message use the same search.

  • os_run(parallelize = TRUE) now checks the running Julia session before calling Omniscape, and warns and runs serially if it cannot run in parallel: if Julia has only one thread, or if it was started with an interactive thread (e.g. JULIA_NUM_THREADS = "4" rather than "4,0"), which makes Omniscape releases before 0.6.3 fail with a BoundsError. This can happen when Julia is started outside cs_setup(), for example by another package.

  • cs_setup() now records the number of threads Julia actually has, and warns when threads cannot take effect because Julia was already running (including when started outside circuitscaper). Previously it recorded the requested count, and os_run(parallelize = TRUE) could reset the record to 1 when it started Julia.

  • os_run() now has Omniscape write its outputs as ASCII grids rather than GeoTIFFs. Writing GeoTIFFs from Julia could crash R (seen on Ubuntu, in TIFFClose), most likely because Julia’s GDAL loads its own libtiff into a process where R’s terra has already loaded the system one. Inputs were already passed as ASCII grids, so Julia now never touches libtiff. Files kept via output_dir are therefore .asc rather than .tif.

  • os_run() now stops with a clear error if the resistance or conductance surface contains zero or negative values, which Omniscape rejects without writing outputs. Previously this surfaced as an obscure failure to read Omniscape’s output.

circuitscaper 0.1.1

CRAN release: 2026-10-01

New features

  • New os_condition() constructor gives os_run() full access to Omniscape’s conditional connectivity (#2):
    • "within" comparisons with user-specified bounds (lower, upper).
    • Present-vs-future comparisons (future), in which sources’ present-day values are compared against targets’ future values, as in climate-tracking connectivity analyses.
    • Two simultaneous conditions, by passing a list of two os_condition() objects.
  • os_run() now warns when a condition layer has missing values at source cells, which Omniscape does not filter.
  • All cs_*() functions and os_run() now warn if the installed Circuitscape.jl or Omniscape.jl does not recognize a configuration option written by circuitscaper, rather than letting the option silently have no effect.

Bug fixes

  • In 0.1.0, os_run()’s condition_type argument was written to the Omniscape configuration under a key Omniscape does not recognize, so it was silently ignored. All conditional analyses instead used Omniscape’s defaults, "within" with bounds of 0 and 0: a source was connected to a target only if its condition value exactly equaled the median value of the target block. This was neither the documented behavior (an unbounded range) nor the requested "equal" comparison. Results from 0.1.0 that used condition should be rerun.
  • In 0.1.0, four_neighbors = TRUE was written to the Circuitscape configuration under an unrecognized key and silently ignored in cs_pairwise(), cs_one_to_all(), cs_all_to_one(), and cs_advanced(); all analyses used 8-neighbor connectivity. Results from 0.1.0 that used four_neighbors = TRUE should be rerun.

Breaking changes and deprecations

  • Passing a raster directly as os_run(condition = ) is now shorthand for os_condition(x, type = "equal"). Use os_condition() for "within" comparisons, which now require explicit bounds.
  • os_run()’s condition_type argument is deprecated. condition_type = "equal" still works with a warning; condition_type = "within" now errors, since it has no way to specify bounds.
